newsitem.title: CHINA: China, S.Korea silent on Pyongyang defector's fate.
newsitem.headline: China, S.Korea silent on Pyongyang defector's fate.

text.p: Chinese and South Korean officials in Beijing remained silent on Monday about the fate of a top Pyongyang defector as speculation grew that his departure from Seoul's heavily guarded mission in Beijing may be imminent.
South Korean embassy officials declined to comment on the whereabouts of Hwang Jang-yop, a senior North Korean ideologue who sought refuge in Seoul's consular compound in Beijing on February 12.
"At this moment I cannot say when he will leave," embassy spokesman Chang Moon-Ik said by telephone.
Chang said Hwang would probably leave China for a third country but declined to identify his likely destination.
Other embassy officials declined to comment when asked if Hwang was still in Beijing.

However, security around Seoul's consulate was tight on Monday. Chinese police armed with assault rifles were posted at approaches to the compound, backed by several armoured personnel carriers and a crowd control truck.
South Korean state radio said Hwang may leave China as early as Monday for the Philippines and that Seoul's ambassador to Beijing Chung Chong-wook had bade him farewell.
A Seoul foreign ministry spokesman declined to comment on the report. "We have decided not to talk about Hwang's whereabouts or the timing of his departure," he said.

China's Foreign Ministry also refused to comment on Hwang's fate, saying they could report no new developments since Premier Li Peng said last Friday that conditions were nearly ripe for a solution to the diplomatic crisis.
The defection of Hwang, the most senior official to abandon his Stalinist homeland, has muddied ties between China and the two Koreas, bitter rivals since the 1950-1953 Korean War.
Beijing must decide whether to hand over Hwang to new business partner Seoul while giving full consideration to the concerns of old communist ally Pyongyang.

In Seoul, another South Korean foreign ministry official said Beijing and Seoul had agreed that Hwang, a senior aide to supreme leader Kim Jong-Il, would be sent to a third country before being allowed asylum in South Korea.
He said the Philippines was one of several "transit points" being considered.
In Tokyo, Japanese Foreign Minister Yukihiko Ikeda said after talks on Monday with his visiting Philippine counterpart he was unable to confirm reports that Hwang had left China for the Philippines.
This view was echoed by Philippine Foreign Secretary Domingo Siazon, who also who is on a five-day visit to Tokyo. He also said there could be alternatives apart from Manila.
Asked if Hwang was now heading for the Philippines as some media reports suggested on Monday, Siazon said:"I don't know."
Siazon said on Saturday his country had been asked to serve as a transit point for Hwang if he were allowed to leave for South Korea.

The South Korean state radio report said Hwang was expected to spend a month in Subic Bay, a former U.S. naval base north of Manila and now a free port with an international airport, before being brought to South Korea.
A top Manila Foreign Office official said Hwang would very likely stay in the Philippines for a few days, but added that it was possible that his country was being used as a decoy.
